content: Epidemiological studies have suggested a potential association between the use of beta₂-agonists and an increased risk of asthma-related mortality. This has led to significant debate regarding whether long-term use of long-acting beta₂-agonists (LABAs), particularly in combination with inhaled corticosteroids (ICSs), is safe. This updated Cochrane Review includes data from two large trials involving 11,679 adults and 6,208 children, both mandated by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), to address these concerns. The objective of this review was to evaluate the risks of mortality and non-fatal serious adverse events (SAEs) in individuals with chronic asthma who were randomized to receive regular salmeterol combined with ICS versus the same dose of ICS alone. The review included randomized trials of at least 12 weeks' duration, involving adults and children with asthma of any severity. Data were collected from trial sponsors, ClinicalTrials.gov, and FDA submissions, and the quality of evidence was assessed using GRADE methodology. A total of 41 studies involving 27,951 adults and adolescents, and eight studies involving 8,453 children, were included in the analysis. Most adults (except 542 participants) and none of the children received salmeterol and fluticasone in a combination inhaler. The overall risk of bias for all-cause events was judged to be low, and data on SAEs were obtained from all study authors. Mortality: Among 14,233 adults treated with regular salmeterol and ICS, 11 deaths occurred, compared to 13 deaths among 13,718 adults treated with ICS alone. The pooled Peto odds ratio (OR) was 0.80 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36 to 1.78), indicating no significant difference in mortality risk between the two groups. For every 1,000 adults treated for 25 weeks, one death occurred in both groups (95% CI 0 to 2 deaths). No deaths were reported among children in either treatment group. Additionally, no deaths due to asthma were reported in adults or children, leaving uncertainty about the impact of these treatments on asthma-related mortality. Non-Fatal Serious Adverse Events (SAEs): In adults, 332 individuals receiving regular salmeterol with ICS experienced a non-fatal SAE of any cause, compared to 282 individuals receiving ICS alone. The pooled Peto OR was 1.14 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.33). For every 1,000 adults treated for 25 weeks, 21 adults on ICS alone experienced an SAE, compared to 23 adults on salmeterol and ICS (95% CI 20 to 27). In children, 65 out of 4,229 receiving regular salmeterol with ICS experienced a non-fatal SAE, compared to 62 out of 4,224 receiving ICS alone. The pooled Peto OR was 1.04 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.48). For every 1,000 children treated for 23 weeks, 15 children on ICS alone experienced an SAE, compared to 15 children on salmeterol and ICS (95% CI 11 to 22). Asthma-Related Serious Adverse Events: In adults, 80 individuals receiving salmeterol and ICS experienced an asthma-related non-fatal SAE, compared to 67 individuals receiving ICS alone. The pooled Peto OR was 1.15 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.59). For every 1,000 adults treated for 25 weeks, five adults on ICS alone experienced an asthma-related SAE, compared to six adults on salmeterol and ICS (95% CI 4 to 8). In children, 29 individuals receiving salmeterol and ICS experienced an asthma-related SAE, compared to 23 individuals receiving ICS alone. The pooled Peto OR was 1.25 (95% CI 0.72 to 2.16). For every 1,000 children treated for 23 weeks, five children on ICS alone experienced an asthma-related SAE, compared to seven children on salmeterol and ICS (95% CI 4 to 12). Authors' Conclusions: The review found no significant difference in the risk of death or serious adverse events between adults and children treated with regular salmeterol and ICS versus ICS alone. Importantly, no asthma-related deaths were reported among the 27,951 adults or 8,453 children included in the trials over an average of six months. This suggests that the risk of dying from asthma while on either treatment is very low. However, uncertainty remains regarding whether adding salmeterol to ICS alters the risk of asthma-related mortality. The inclusion of new trials has improved the precision of estimates for non-fatal SAEs. Based on the worst-case scenario, at least 152 adults and 139 children would need to be treated with combination salmeterol and ICS for six months for one additional person to experience a non-fatal SAE requiring hospitalization, compared to treatment with ICS alone. These potential risks must be weighed against the benefits of combination therapy. It is also worth noting that adherence to prescribed treatment exceeded 90% in the new trials, which may differ from adherence rates in real-world clinical practice.
